metadata.description: Estimate recommended life insurance coverage using the income replacement method.

keywords: how much life insurance do i need

faqs.question: How much life insurance do I need?
faqs.answer: A common rule of thumb is 10-15 times your income, but a better approach is to calculate your needs: outstanding debts (mortgage, loans) + future expenses (college, living costs) - existing resources (savings, current coverage). The difference is the coverage you need.

faqs.question: What is the difference between term and whole life insurance?
faqs.answer: Term life provides a death benefit for a specific period (10-30 years) and is cheaper. Whole life covers you for your entire life and builds cash value, but premiums are 5-10 times higher. Most people only need term life.

faqs.question: How are life insurance premiums calculated?
faqs.answer: Premiums are based on age, health, coverage amount, policy type, and habits (smokers pay more). Younger, healthier individuals get lower rates. With term life, rates are locked in for the duration of the policy.

faqs.question: Do I need life insurance through work?
faqs.answer: Employer-provided coverage is usually insufficient (often only 1-2 times your income). If you have dependents, add an individual policy to cover the gap. Individual policies stay with you when you change jobs.

metadata.title: Medicare Cost Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate annual Medicare costs, including premiums, IRMAA surcharges, and out-of-pocket expenses.

faqs.question: How much does Medicare cost in 2026?
faqs.answer: Most people pay $0 for Part A, and Part B is $202.90/month (standard premium). Part D averages about $39/month. Total baseline: about $242/month. Higher earners pay more due to IRMAA surcharges — up to $689.90/month for Part B alone at the highest income tier.

faqs.question: What is IRMAA?
faqs.answer: IRMAA (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount) is a surcharge added to Part B and Part D premiums for higher-income beneficiaries. It is based on your MAGI from 2 years ago (2026 premiums use 2024 income). IRMAA kicks in starting at $109,001 for singles and $218,001 for married filing jointly. The highest tier (single $500K+, joint $750K+) adds $487/month to Part B and $91/month to Part D.

faqs.question: Is Medicare Part A really free?
faqs.answer: Part A is premium-free if you (or your spouse) worked and paid Medicare taxes for more than 40 quarters (10 years). With 30-39 quarters, you pay $311/month. Fewer than 30 quarters: $565/month. However, Part A still has a $1,736 deductible per benefit period, plus daily copays beyond 60 days.

faqs.question: What does Medicare Part B cover?
faqs.answer: Part B covers doctor visits, outpatient care, preventive services, medical equipment, ambulance services, mental health, and some home health care. After the $283 annual deductible, you typically pay 20% coinsurance with no out-of-pocket maximum — which is why many people buy Medigap supplemental coverage.

faqs.question: What is the Part D out-of-pocket cap?
faqs.answer: Starting in 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act set the Part D out-of-pocket cap at $2,000 per year ($2,100 in 2026). Once you reach this cap, you pay $0 for covered drugs for the rest of the year. This is a major change — previously there was no annual cap and costs could spiral.

faqs.question: What is Medigap?
faqs.answer: Medigap (Medicare Supplement) plans are private insurance that covers the gaps in Original Medicare — copays, coinsurance, and deductibles. Plan G is the most popular, typically $100-$250/month depending on age, location, and insurer. Medigap only works with Original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage.

faqs.question: What happens if I delay enrolling in Medicare?
faqs.answer: Part B: a 10% premium surcharge for every full 12 months you were eligible but did not enroll — permanently. Part D: 1% of the base premium for every uncovered month ($0.39/month in 2026) — also permanent. These penalties add up fast: delaying Part B by 3 years means paying 30% more for life.

faqs.question: When can I enroll in Medicare?
faqs.answer: Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months: it begins 3 months before your 65th birthday month, includes your birthday month, and ends 3 months after. You can also enroll during the General Enrollment Period (January 1-March 31, with coverage starting July 1) or during a Special Enrollment Period if you have a qualifying event.

whatIs.title: Understanding Medicare Costs
whatIs.content: Medicare has several cost components: Part A (hospital), Part B (medical/outpatient), Part D (prescription drugs), and optional Medigap supplemental coverage. Most people pay $0 for Part A if they have more than 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment. Parts B and D have standard premiums, which are increased by IRMAA surcharges for higher earners.

metadata.description: Calculate how much extra monthly payments can shorten your term and save in interest.

faqs.question: How can I pay off my mortgage faster?
faqs.answer: Strategies: 1) Biweekly payments (one extra payment per year), 2) add 1/12 to each monthly payment, 3) make one extra lump-sum payment per year, 4) round payments up to the next $100. Any method saves thousands in interest.

faqs.question: Should I refinance or make extra payments?
faqs.answer: Refinancing is worth it if rates are more than 1% lower. Otherwise, extra payments are better — no closing costs and immediate interest savings. Refinancing resets your term (unless you choose a 15-year).

faqs.question: How do extra payments save interest?
faqs.answer: Extra payments directly reduce the principal, shrinking the amount that accrues interest. A $100 extra payment on a 30-year, 4% loan saves about $180 in interest. Over time, the compounding savings are significant.

faqs.question: Are there prepayment penalties?
faqs.answer: Some loans have them — especially in the early years. Check your promissory note. Most conventional loans have no penalty. If the penalty exceeds the savings, avoid extra payments until the penalty period ends.

metadata.title: Net Worth Percentile Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate your net worth percentile by country.

keywords: how much should i have saved

faqs.question: What is the median net worth in the U.S.?
faqs.answer: The median U.S. household net worth is approximately $192,700. The average (mean) is much higher at about $1,060,000 because extremely wealthy households pull the average up. Median is a better measure of the 'typical' American's wealth.

faqs.question: What net worth makes you top 1%?
faqs.answer: A net worth of roughly $13 million or more puts you in the top 1% of U.S. households. The threshold varies by age: for under-35 households it's around $1.5M, while for 55-64 year olds it's around $15M.

faqs.question: What should my net worth be at my age?
faqs.answer: A common guideline is to have 1x your annual salary saved by 30, 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, and 10x by 67. However, these are rough targets. The median net worth by age group gives a more realistic picture of where Americans actually stand.

faqs.question: Does net worth include home equity?
faqs.answer: Yes. Net worth equals total assets minus total debts. Assets include home equity, retirement accounts, savings, investments, vehicles, and other property. Debts include mortgages, student loans, auto loans, credit cards, and any other liabilities.

faqs.question: Why is average net worth so much higher than median?
faqs.answer: The top 10% of households hold about 70% of all wealth. A few extremely wealthy families (with net worths in the billions) dramatically pull the average upward, making it unrepresentative of typical Americans. The median (50th percentile) is the point where exactly half of households have more and half have less.

faqs.question: How does net worth vary by age?
faqs.answer: Net worth generally increases with age due to accumulated savings, home equity, and investment growth. The median rises from about $39,000 for under-35 to $410,000 for ages 65-74, then declines slightly to $336,000 for 75+ as retirees draw down savings.

faqs.question: What is Ohm's Law?
faqs.answer: Ohm's Law states that voltage = current × resistance (V = IR). It describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit. If you know two of them, you can calculate the third.

faqs.question: How do I calculate power?
faqs.answer: Power (watts) = voltage × current (P = VI). Using Ohm's Law to substitute: P = I²R or P = V²/R. This is used for electrical systems and appliance ratings.

faqs.question: What happens to current if resistance increases?
faqs.answer: At constant voltage, current decreases as resistance increases (I = V/R). Doubling the resistance means half the current. This is why long extension cords (higher resistance) reduce current to devices.

faqs.question: Why is Ohm's Law important?
faqs.answer: It is the foundation of all electrical engineering. Designing circuits, selecting fuses, wiring, and ensuring appliances receive the right power all rely on Ohm's Law. Without it, electrical systems would be unpredictable and dangerous.

metadata.title: Personal Injury Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate personal injury settlement amounts based on medical bills, lost wages, and a pain multiplier.

faqs.question: How are personal injury settlements calculated?
faqs.answer: Insurance companies use the "multiplier method" as a starting point. Your total medical expenses are multiplied by a factor (1.5x for minor injuries, up to 10x for catastrophic injuries) to estimate pain and suffering. Lost wages and property damage are added separately. The result is then adjusted by your percentage of fault according to your state's negligence rules and is limited by the defendant's insurance policy limits.

faqs.question: What is the pain and suffering multiplier?
faqs.answer: The multiplier is a number (typically 1.5 to 10) applied to your medical bills to estimate non-economic damages such as pain, suffering, mental anguish, and loss of enjoyment of life. Minor soft tissue injuries use 1.5-3x, moderate injuries like fractures use 3-5x, serious injuries requiring surgery use 5-7x, and catastrophic or permanent injuries use 7-10x or higher.

faqs.question: What is comparative negligence?
faqs.answer: Comparative negligence reduces your settlement by your percentage of fault. In "pure comparative" states (like CA and NY), you can recover even at 99% fault. In "modified comparative" states, you are barred from recovery at 50% or 51% fault, depending on the state. In "pure contributory" states (AL, MD, NC, VA, DC), you are barred from any recovery even at just 1% fault.

faqs.question: How do insurance policy limits affect my settlement?
faqs.answer: The defendant's insurance policy limits are usually the practical ceiling on your recovery, regardless of your case's theoretical value. If your case is worth $500,000 but the defendant only has $50,000 in liability coverage, you will likely only collect $50,000 unless the defendant has substantial personal assets. Your own underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage can make up the difference.

faqs.question: Does having surgery increase my settlement?
faqs.answer: Yes, significantly. Cases involving surgery typically settle for 2-5 times more than cases with conservative treatment only. Surgery provides objective evidence of injury severity and proves that less invasive treatment was insufficient.

faqs.question: What if I have a pre-existing condition?
faqs.answer: Under the "eggshell plaintiff" doctrine, the defendant takes you as they find you — if a minor collision causes serious injury because of a pre-existing condition, the defendant is still liable. However, insurance adjusters will argue your treatment was for the pre-existing condition rather than the accident. The key is proving the accident caused a flare-up or worsening of your condition.

faqs.question: Do most states cap pain and suffering damages?
faqs.answer: No. Most states do not cap non-economic damages in general personal injury cases. Only about 4 states have enforceable general personal injury damage caps (CO, MD, OH, TN). More states cap damages specifically for medical malpractice cases, but those caps do not apply to car accidents, slip and falls, or other general injury claims.

faqs.question: Should I hire a lawyer for my injury claim?
faqs.answer: Research consistently shows that represented claimants recover 3-3.5 times more than unrepresented claimants, even after attorney fees (typically 33-40% on contingency). For minor soft tissue injuries with clear liability and low medical bills, you may be able to handle the claim yourself. For moderate to severe injuries, surgery cases, liability disputes, or cases involving permanent impairment, an attorney will almost certainly increase your net recovery.

whatIs.title: How the Personal Injury Calculator Works
whatIs.content: This calculator uses the multiplier method to estimate your personal injury settlement, the standard approach insurance adjusters and personal injury attorneys use to evaluate claims.

sections.heading: The Formula
sections.content: Your medical expenses (called "specials") are multiplied by a factor based on injury severity to estimate pain and suffering ("generals"). Lost wages and property damage are added as separate economic damages. Formula: settlement = medical bills + (medical bills × multiplier) + lost wages + property damage

sections.heading: State Negligence Rules
sections.content: Your state's negligence laws determine how fault affects your recovery. Pure comparative negligence states allow recovery at any fault level (reduced proportionally). Modified comparative states bar recovery at 50% or 51% fault. Five jurisdictions (AL, MD, NC, VA, DC) use pure contributory negligence, which bars any recovery even at 1% fault.

tips.title: Why Results Are Estimates
tips.content: Insurance companies use proprietary software (like Colossus) that considers hundreds of factors. The multiplier method is a simplified version of what that software does. Actual settlements depend on the specific facts of your case, the quality of evidence, the jurisdiction, the judge or jury, whether you have an attorney, and the defendant's insurance coverage.

faqs.question: What is RAP?
faqs.answer: RAP (Random Additional Payments) are extra payments made beyond your regular loan payment. They directly reduce the principal, accelerating repayment and saving interest. Same as extra payments, but the terminology varies by lender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between RAP and extra payments?
faqs.answer: None — they are the same thing. RAP is just the term some lenders use. Both reduce the principal, shorten the loan term, and save interest.

faqs.question: Should I save or pay RAP?
faqs.answer: If your loan rate is higher than your savings rate, pay RAP. If the loan rate is lower than investment returns, invest the difference. Rule of thumb: if the rate is > 6%, prioritize the debt; if it is < 4%, prioritize investing.

faqs.question: How does RAP affect my loan?
faqs.answer: RAP reduces the outstanding balance, lowering future interest. Some lenders recalculate your payment (lowering it), while others shorten the term (keeping payments the same). Designate the payment to be applied to principal.

faqs.question: What is self-employment tax?
faqs.answer: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax for self-employed workers. In 2026, the rate is 15.3% of net earnings (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare). You pay both the employer and employee shares.

faqs.question: How much income is subject to self-employment tax?
faqs.answer: Social Security tax applies to net earnings up to $176,100 (2026). Medicare tax applies to all net earnings. An additional 0.9% Medicare tax applies above $200,000 (single).

faqs.question: Can I deduct self-employment tax?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can deduct the employer-equivalent portion (7.65% of net earnings) as an above-the-line deduction. This reduces your income tax, but not the self-employment tax itself.

faqs.question: Do LLC owners pay self-employment tax?
faqs.answer: Yes, unless you elect S corporation status. A single-member LLC is treated as a disregarded entity — you pay self-employment tax. S corp owners pay FICA tax only on their salary (not distributions), which can save money.

metadata.title: Small Claims Court Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate small claims court filing and service fees based on your claim amount.

faqs.question: What is small claims court?
faqs.answer: Small claims court is a simplified legal process for resolving disputes involving relatively small amounts of money. The rules are designed for people without lawyers — hearings are informal, there is no jury, and cases are usually decided the same day. Amount limits range from $2,500 (Kentucky) to $25,000 (Tennessee, Delaware). Filing fees are typically $25-$150.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer in small claims court?
faqs.answer: In most cases, no — in 13 states (including California, Arizona, Colorado, Michigan, and Washington), attorneys are actually prohibited from representing parties in small claims court. The court is designed for self-representation. However, in states that allow lawyers, one side having an attorney can put the other at a disadvantage.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations?
faqs.answer: The statute of limitations is the deadline for filing a claim after an event occurs. It varies by state and claim type. For example, Kentucky gives you only 1 year for personal injury claims, while Maine allows 6 years. Written contracts usually have longer deadlines (3-15 years) than personal injury claims (1-6 years). Missing this deadline means your case is dismissed.

faqs.question: What if my claim exceeds the small claims limit?
faqs.answer: You have three options: (1) reduce your claim to the small claims limit and waive the rest, (2) file in regular civil court (more expensive and complex), or (3) in some states, split the claim into multiple cases (though many states prohibit this). If the excess is small relative to civil court costs, option 1 is usually the best choice.

faqs.question: Can I appeal a small claims decision?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Most states allow either party to appeal, usually within 10-30 days. California and Massachusetts only allow the defendant to appeal. Arizona does not allow small claims appeals at all. Appeals are usually "trial de novo" (a brand-new trial) in a higher court.

faqs.question: Where do I file a small claims case?
faqs.answer: Almost always in the county or district where the defendant lives or does business, or where the incident occurred (where the contract was signed, where the property was damaged, etc.). Filing in the wrong location can result in dismissal.

faqs.question: Which states have the highest and lowest limits?
faqs.answer: Highest: Tennessee and Delaware ($25,000), Texas and Utah ($20,000), Georgia, Minnesota, and North Dakota ($15,000). Lowest: Kentucky ($2,500), Arizona and Mississippi ($3,500), Nebraska ($3,900), Kansas ($4,000). California allows $12,500 for individuals but only $6,250 for businesses.

faqs.question: How long does small claims court take?
faqs.answer: It typically takes 30-75 days from filing to the hearing. The hearing itself usually takes 15-60 minutes, and you get a decision that day or within a few days. If you win, collecting the judgment can take longer — the court does not collect it for you.

whatIs.title: What Is Small Claims Court?
whatIs.content: Small claims court is a simplified legal process for resolving disputes involving relatively small amounts of money. The rules are designed for people without lawyers — hearings are informal, there is no jury, and cases are usually decided the same day. Amount limits range from $2,500 (Kentucky) to $25,000 (Tennessee, Delaware).

Lowest: Kentucky ($2,500), Arizona and Mississippi ($3,500), Nebraska ($3,900), Kansas ($4,000). California allows $12,500 for individuals but only $6,250 for businesses.

sections.heading: Filing Fees and Statutes of Limitations
sections.content: Filing fees are typically $25-$150, varying by state and claim amount. The statute of limitations (deadline to file) varies by state and claim type. Written contracts usually have longer deadlines (3-15 years) than personal injury claims (1-6 years).

sections.content: In most cases, no lawyer is needed — in 13 states (including California, Arizona, Colorado, Michigan, and Washington), attorneys are actually prohibited from representing parties in small claims court. The court is designed for self-representation.

tips.content: Rules and fees vary by county/jurisdiction within each state. Always check with your local court clerk before filing. metadata.title: Social Security Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate Social Security retirement benefits based on AIME and claiming age.

faqs.question: How is Social Security calculated?
faqs.answer: The SSA takes your 35 highest-earning years, adjusts them for inflation (indexes them), calculates your Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME), then applies a three-tier formula: 90% of the first $1,286, plus 32% of earnings between $1,286 and $7,749, plus 15% of earnings above $7,749 (2026 bend points). The result is your Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) — your monthly benefit at Full Retirement Age.

faqs.question: What is Full Retirement Age?
faqs.answer: Full Retirement Age (FRA) is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For those born 1955-1959, it gradually increases from 66 years and 2 months to 66 years and 10 months. At FRA, you receive 100% of your PIA, with no reduction or increase.

faqs.question: How much less will I get at 62?
faqs.answer: Claiming at 62 (with an FRA of 67) reduces your benefit by 30%. This reduction is permanent — it does not recover when you reach 67. For example, if your PIA is $2,000/month, you receive $1,400/month for life if you claim at 62.

faqs.question: How much more will I get at 70?
faqs.answer: Waiting until 70 earns delayed retirement credits of 8% per year past FRA. With an FRA of 67, waiting until 70 gives you 124% of your PIA. A $2,000 PIA becomes $2,480/month. No additional credits accrue after 70.

faqs.question: Are Social Security benefits taxable?
faqs.answer: Depending on your total income, up to 85% of your benefits may be taxable. If your combined income (AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your SS benefits) exceeds $25,000 (single) or $32,000 (married filing jointly), part of your benefits is taxable. Below these thresholds, benefits are tax-free.

faqs.question: What are spousal benefits?
faqs.answer: A spouse can receive up to 50% of the higher earner's PIA at FRA, if that is higher than their own benefit. The higher earner must already be claiming. Spousal benefits can be claimed as early as 62 (at a reduced rate). Spousal benefits earn no delayed retirement credits — there is no advantage to waiting past FRA.

faqs.question: What is the maximum Social Security benefit in 2026?
faqs.answer: The maximum monthly benefit in 2026 is $2,969 at 62, $4,152 at FRA, and $5,181 at 70. To get the maximum, you need to earn at or above the taxable maximum ($184,500 in 2026) in each of your 35 highest-earning years.

faqs.question: What if I work fewer than 35 years?
faqs.answer: The SSA always uses 35 years. If you work fewer than 35 years, zero-income years fill the gaps, dragging down your average. Each missing year reduces your AIME by 1/35. Even a few more years of work can significantly increase your benefit if they replace zero years.

whatIs.title: How Social Security Benefits Are Calculated
whatIs.content: Social Security retirement benefits are calculated using your 35 highest-earning years, adjusted for inflation (indexed), to determine your Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME). A three-tier formula then calculates your Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) — your monthly benefit at Full Retirement Age. The 2026 bend points are $1,286 and $7,749.

howTo.title: The PIA Formula and Claiming Age

sections.heading: 1. Calculate AIME
sections.content: The SSA takes your 35 highest-earning years (capped at the taxable maximum, $184,500 in 2026), indexes them for inflation, and divides by 420 months (35 years) to get your Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME). If you worked fewer than 35 years, zero-income years fill the gaps.

sections.heading: 2. Apply the PIA Formula
sections.content: 2026 formula: 90% of the first $1,286 of AIME, plus 32% of AIME between $1,286 and $7,749, plus 15% of AIME above $7,749. The result is your Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) — your monthly benefit at Full Retirement Age.

sections.heading: 3. Adjust for Claiming Age
sections.content: Claiming before Full Retirement Age (67 for those born in 1960 or later) permanently reduces benefits — by 30% at 62. Claiming after FRA earns delayed retirement credits of 8% per year up to 70 (124% of PIA). No additional credits accrue after 70.

tips.title: Important Considerations
tips.content: This calculator provides a simplified estimate using the 2026 bend points and does not perform full wage indexing. Actual benefits depend on your complete earnings history, including year-by-year inflation adjustments. For a precise estimate, use the my Social Security account at ssa.gov. Benefits are subject to federal income tax if your combined income exceeds $25,000 (single) or $32,000 (married filing jointly).

faqs.question: What is the student loan tax bomb?
faqs.answer: When student loans are forgiven or discharged, the forgiven amount may be treated as taxable income. For example, $50,000 forgiven under an IDR plan after 20 years could result in a $10,000-$12,000 tax bill.

faqs.question: Is all loan forgiveness taxable?
faqs.answer: No. PSLF (Public Service Loan Forgiveness) is tax-free. Teacher forgiveness is also tax-free. From 2021-2025, certain federal loan forgiveness was tax-free under COVID relief. IDR forgiveness after 20 years is generally taxable.

faqs.question: How can I prepare for the tax bomb?
faqs.answer: Estimate your forgiveness amount and save into an investment account. If $50,000 is forgiven, save $200-300 per month into a taxable account. Alternatively, adjust your income-driven repayment plan to avoid a large forgiveness event.

faqs.question: Is there a way to avoid the tax bomb?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pursue PSLF (tax-free forgiveness after 10 years). File separately if married (may reduce the taxable amount). Or adjust your IDR plan to minimize forgiveness.

faqs.answer: The government deposits $1,000 for each newborn. Parents can contribute up to an additional $5,000 per year (same limit as an IRA). Funds are invested in index funds and grow tax-free. At age 18, the child takes control of the account.

faqs.answer: Assuming a 7% annual return: $1,000 initial + $1,000 yearly contributions for 18 years = about $40,000. Government-only $1,000 for 18 years = about $3,400.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Trump Account and a 529 plan?
faqs.answer: A 529 plan is specifically for education expenses; withdrawals for non-education purposes are taxed and penalized. A Trump Account can be used for any purpose — education, a home, a business, or retirement. Both offer tax-free growth.

metadata.title: VA Disability Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate your combined disability rating and monthly VA disability compensation (with dependents).

faqs.question: How does VA math work?
faqs.answer: The VA does not add ratings together. Instead, each disability reduces your remaining "whole person" efficiency. Start at 100% healthy. A 70% rating leaves 30%. A second 50% rating takes 50% of the remaining 30% (=15%), leaving 15%. So 70% + 50% = 85% combined (not 120%), rounded to 90%. This is why two 50% ratings equal 75%, not 100%.

faqs.question: How does VA rounding work?
faqs.answer: The VA rounds the combined rating to the nearest 10%. Values ending in 5 or higher round up: 75% → 80%, 65% → 70%. Values ending in 4 or lower round down: 74% → 70%, 64% → 60%. This rounding can make a significant difference in monthly compensation.

faqs.question: When do I get dependent allowances?
faqs.answer: You must have a combined rating of 30% or higher to receive additional compensation for dependents (spouse, children, dependent parents). At 10% and 20%, you receive only the basic veteran rate regardless of dependents.

faqs.question: What is TDIU?
faqs.answer: Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) pays at the 100% rate even when your combined rating is below 100%, if you cannot maintain substantially gainful employment due to your service-connected disabilities. Eligibility: one disability at 60%+, or multiple disabilities combined at 70%+ with at least one at 40%+.

faqs.question: Are VA disability payments taxable?
faqs.answer: No. VA disability compensation is completely tax-free at both the federal and state level. A $3,828 monthly payment at 100% is equivalent to roughly $5,000 per month in taxable income, depending on your tax rate.

faqs.question: What is the bilateral factor?
faqs.answer: When disabilities affect paired extremities (both arms, both legs), the VA first combines those ratings, then adds 10% of that combined value before combining with other disabilities. This slightly increases the overall combined rating.

faqs.question: How often do VA rates change?
faqs.answer: VA compensation rates are adjusted annually based on the Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA), the same increase applied to Social Security. The 2026 rates (effective December 1, 2025) reflect a 2.5% COLA increase.

faqs.question: What is Special Monthly Compensation?
faqs.answer: SMC provides additional payments beyond the standard rating for severe disabilities. SMC-K (about $140/month) is the most common, for loss of reproductive organs, a hand, a foot, or an eye. SMC-S (about $4,215/month) is for housebound veterans. Higher levels (L through R) can exceed $11,000/month for veterans needing extensive personal care.

whatIs.title: The VA Combined Rating Formula
whatIs.content: The VA does not add disability ratings together. Instead, each disability reduces your remaining "whole person" efficiency. The VA starts at 100% healthy and subtracts each disability rating as a percentage of what remains. The final combined rating is rounded to the nearest 10%.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content: Example: combining 50% + 30%. Start at 100%. Apply 50%: 100 × 50% = 50, leaving 50%. Apply 30%: 50 × 30% = 15, leaving 35%. Combined: 100 - 35 = 65%. Rounded to the nearest 10%: 70%.

sections.heading: Rounding Rules
sections.content: The VA rounds the combined rating to the nearest 10%. Values ending in 5 or higher round up (65% → 70%, 75% → 80%). Values ending in 4 or lower round down (64% → 60%, 74% → 70%).

sections.heading: 2026 Compensation Rates
sections.content: Rates effective December 1, 2025 (2.5% COLA). They range from $175.51/month at 10% to $3,828.06/month at 100%. All VA disability compensation is completely tax-free at the federal and state level.

tips.title: Dependents and TDIU
tips.content: You must have a combined rating of 30% or higher to receive additional compensation for dependents (spouse, children, dependent parents). TDIU (Total Disability Individual Unemployability) pays at the 100% rate even when your combined rating is below 100%, if you cannot maintain substantially gainful employment due to your service-connected disabilities.

metadata.title: Workers' Comp Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate workers' compensation benefits based on weekly wage and disability level.

faqs.question: How much does workers' comp pay?
faqs.answer: Most states pay 66.67% (two-thirds) of your average weekly wage (AWW) as temporary total disability (TTD). A few states use different rates: Massachusetts and New Hampshire pay 60%, New Jersey, Oklahoma, and Texas pay 70%, and Connecticut, Rhode Island, Alaska, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan use 75-80% of after-tax wages. All states have weekly benefit maximums — ranging from $631 in Mississippi to $2,350 in Iowa.

faqs.question: Is workers' comp taxable?
faqs.answer: No. Workers' compensation benefits are not subject to federal income tax. However, if you also receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), some SSDI benefits may become taxable if your workers' comp + SSDI total exceeds 80% of your pre-injury earnings. All states follow the federal exemption for state tax purposes.

faqs.question: What is the waiting period?
faqs.answer: The waiting period is the number of days after an injury before wage-replacement benefits begin (medical treatment is covered from day one). Most states have a 3-day or 7-day waiting period. If your disability exceeds the "retroactive period" (usually 14-21 days), the waiting period is paid retroactively.

faqs.question: What are monopolistic states?
faqs.answer: Four states require employers to buy workers' comp exclusively from a state fund (no private insurers): Ohio (BWC), Washington (L&I), Wyoming (DWS), and North Dakota (WSI). This does not affect your benefits — it just means the state, rather than a private insurer, administers claims.

faqs.question: Can my employer opt out of workers' comp?
faqs.answer: Texas is the only state where workers' comp is truly voluntary. Employers who opt out ("nonsubscribers") lose certain legal protections, and injured workers can sue them without the usual defenses. Oklahoma had an opt-out system starting in 2013, but it was ruled unconstitutional in 2016. In all other states, coverage is mandatory.

faqs.question: What is the difference between TTD, TPD, PPD, and PTD?
faqs.answer: TTD (temporary total disability) is paid when you are completely unable to work during recovery — this is what the calculator estimates. TPD (temporary partial disability) pays partial benefits when you can do light-duty work but at reduced wages. PPD (permanent partial disability) compensates lasting impairment after reaching maximum medical improvement. PTD (permanent total disability) pays ongoing benefits when you can never return to work.

faqs.question: How long do workers' comp benefits last?
faqs.answer: TTD benefits typically last until you can return to work or reach maximum medical improvement (MMI). Most states have no strict time limit on TTD, but some do (Georgia caps it at 400 weeks unless catastrophic). PPD benefits have scheduled durations based on the body part and impairment percentage. PTD benefits may last until retirement age or for life, depending on the state.

faqs.question: Does workers' comp cover medical bills?
faqs.answer: Yes, separately from wage replacement. Workers' comp covers all reasonable and necessary medical treatment related to the work injury — usually with no deductibles, copays, or coverage limits. This includes emergency visits, surgery, physical therapy, prescriptions, and medical equipment. You typically must use approved providers or obtain authorization.

whatIs.title: How the Workers' Comp Calculator Works
whatIs.content: This calculator estimates your temporary total disability (TTD) benefits based on your state's workers' compensation rules. TTD is the most common type of workers' comp benefit — it replaces part of your wages when you cannot work due to a work-related injury or illness.

sections.heading: Calculating the Weekly Benefit
sections.content: Weekly benefit = AWW × state rate (capped by state minimums/maximums). Most states use 66.67% (two-thirds) of your average weekly wage. A few states use a higher percentage of after-tax wages (75-80%), which usually produces a similar amount.

sections.heading: Waiting and Retroactive Periods
sections.content: Every state has a waiting period (3-7 days) before wage benefits begin — medical treatment is covered from day one. If your disability exceeds the retroactive period (usually 14-21 days), the waiting period is paid retroactively, meaning you are compensated for the full time off.

sections.heading: Why Benefits Are Tax-Free
sections.content: Workers' comp benefits are exempt from federal and state income taxes. This means your $800 weekly benefit has the same purchasing power as roughly $1,000-$1,100 in regular wages. When evaluating wage replacement, keep in mind that you keep more of every dollar.

tips.title: Important Notes
tips.content: This calculator only estimates temporary total disability (TTD) benefits. Actual benefits are determined by your state's workers' compensation board based on your verified wage history and medical records. Medical treatment costs are covered separately, with no deductibles or copays.

items: Upload a video (drag & drop or click).
Drag the slider or tap a preset to choose the speed (0.25x–4x).
Click “Change Speed” and download the result when done.

tips.title: Tips
items: After speeding up, the duration is about 1/speed of the original; the same applies when slowing down.
Audio stays in sync with the picture and the pitch is preserved.
Processing happens entirely in your browser; the video is never uploaded.

faqs.question: Why doesn't the audio sound chipmunk-y after speeding up?
faqs.answer: The audio is processed with the atempo filter, which changes speed while preserving the pitch.

faqs.question: How fast or slow can I go?
faqs.answer: From 0.25x to 4x.

faqs.question: Are my videos uploaded?
faqs.answer: No. All processing happens locally in your browser.

metadata.title: Subtitle Burner - Free Online Tool
metadata.description: Free online tool to burn SRT/ASS/VTT subtitles into your video, with optional custom font support. All processing in your browser.

video-subtitle-burner.title: Subtitle Burner
video-subtitle-burner.description: Upload a video and a subtitle file (SRT/ASS/VTT) to burn the subtitles directly into the picture. A custom font is optional. Everything runs locally — nothing is uploaded.

whatIs.title: What is a Subtitle Burner?
body: This tool burns (composites) SRT/ASS/VTT subtitles directly into the video picture, so any player can show them without an external subtitle file. It uses DejaVu Sans by default; for Chinese subtitles we recommend uploading a font that supports CJK glyphs.

howTo.title: How to use
items: Upload a video (drag & drop or click).
Add a subtitle file (SRT / ASS / VTT), and optionally a font (TTF / OTF).
Click “Burn Subtitles” and download the subtitled video when done.

tips.title: Tips
items: Burned subtitles are part of the picture — they display in any player on any platform.
The default font has no CJK glyphs; for Chinese/Japanese/Korean subtitles upload a matching font (e.g. Noto Sans CJK TTF).
The video is re-encoded to H.264 while the audio is copied as-is, so quality loss is minimal.

faqs.question: What is the difference between burned and soft subtitles?
faqs.answer: Burned (hard) subtitles are composited into the picture so any player shows them. Soft subtitles are a separate track that requires player support.

faqs.question: Which subtitle formats are supported?
faqs.answer: SRT, ASS and VTT (WebVTT).

faqs.question: Why do my Chinese subtitles show as boxes?
faqs.answer: The default DejaVu Sans font has no CJK glyphs. Please upload a font that supports Chinese (e.g. Noto Sans CJK TTF).

faqs.question: Are my video and subtitles uploaded?
faqs.answer: No. All processing happens locally in your browser.

faqs.question: Does burning reduce quality?
faqs.answer: The video is re-encoded to H.264 while the audio is copied unchanged, so quality loss is minimal.

metadata.title: Currency Converter - Free Online Tool
metadata.description: Free online currency converter with live exchange rates for 40+ currencies. No signup required — works offline with built-in fallback rates.

currency-converter.title: Currency Converter
currency-converter.description: Convert between 40+ world currencies with live exchange rates. Everything happens right in your browser — no signup, no data sent to us.

whatIs.title: What is a currency converter?
body: This tool converts any amount between 40+ world currencies using live exchange rates. Rates are fetched from free public APIs when you open the page; if the network is unavailable, built-in rates are used instead so the tool keeps working offline.

howTo.title: How to use
items: Enter the amount you want to convert.
Choose the source currency (From) and target currency (To).
Read the converted amount and the unit rate instantly — no button needed.

tips.title: Tips
items: Use the Swap button to flip the currencies — the amount is carried over automatically.
The offline fallback is a snapshot and may be stale; prefer live rates when accuracy matters.
Rates refresh each time you open the page.

faqs.question: How often are the exchange rates updated?
faqs.answer: Rates are fetched from free public APIs (European Central Bank data via frankfurter.app, or open.er-api.com) each time the page loads. ECB rates update once per working day; open.er-api updates daily.

faqs.question: Does it still work offline?
faqs.answer: Yes. If every live API is unreachable, the tool falls back to built-in snapshot rates so you can still convert — just note they may be out of date.

faqs.question: Which currencies are supported?
faqs.answer: Over 40 major currencies, including USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, HKD, KRW and many more.

faqs.question: Is my data sent to a server?
faqs.answer: No. The amount you enter is only processed in your browser. The only network request is to fetch public exchange rates.
